strengths: Addresses an important problem: retaining information beyond a transformer’s context window in offline reinforcement learning.

The T-Maze results provide concrete evidence of useful retention. At corridor length 900, the MRV ablation improves success from 0.61 without MRV to 0.90 with MRV (Table 6). ViZDoom also shows substantial gains over DT.

The evaluation covers several memory tasks, Atari, and MuJoCo, with repeated runs, memory-corruption experiments, and alternative MRV designs. Appendices provide dataset construction, hyperparameters, evaluation details, and a code link.
weaknesses: Important comparison confounds remain unresolved. Appendix D removes feed-forward blocks only from RATE and introduces segment-wise return-target resets for MuJoCo, while baseline scores use their original protocols. Controlled ablations are needed to separate the effects of memory, architecture changes, and return conditioning.

The recurrent baselines are insufficiently validated. DLSTM, DGRU, and DMamba all achieve 0.50 success even at the 90-step T-Maze training length (Table 1). Without adequate tuning details and training-fit diagnostics, these failures do not support the claimed inability of recurrent and state-space models to handle sparse memory tasks.

Novelty is limited: RATE combines established DT tokenization, RMT memory tokens, and Transformer-XL caching, with standard cross-attention as the principal addition. The distinction from existing memory-update mechanisms needs stronger justification. The strongest retention evidence concerns a single cue; memory capacity and more complex information updates remain untested.

Broad superiority is overstated. Memory Maze yields 7.64 ± 0.41 versus RMT’s 7.27 ± 0.21, with only three training runs. On Minigrid, RATE trails TrXL on smaller grids and RMT on larger grids. Its MuJoCo mean of 78.5 also trails both Mamba-based comparators. These results support selective benefits more clearly than general dominance.

Some technical claims are unsupported or inconsistent. The asserted ordering R[OracleDT] ≥ R[RATE] ≥ R[DT] is not guaranteed for separately trained models; OracleDT is an empirical reference, not an established upper bound. Appendix G’s parameter-difference formula omits MRV projections and conflicts with the removal of feed-forward blocks. Algorithm 1 also leaves the hidden-state caching procedure unspecified.
